title: Our Story: How KISWA Was Born
excerpt: KISWA was not planned in a boardroom. It was forged in the fire of crisis, loss, and the unbreakable will of sex workers who refused to be invisible.
content:
KISWA was not planned in a boardroom. It was forged in the fire of crisis, loss, and the unbreakable will of sex workers who refused to be invisible.

A Crisis That Demanded a Response

In Kisumu, sex workers were being brutally killed. Foreign objects were being forced into their bodies. Police made arbitrary arrests. And mainstream organizations — more concerned with filling their databases than actually helping — looked the other way.

There was no organization truly led by sex workers. No one fighting for them with the same urgency, the same lived experience, the same skin in the game. The injustice was relentless, and the silence around it was deafening.

Peer Educators Who Said Enough

From the margins, a group of peer educators gathered. These were sex workers who had been in the community for over eight years — women who had seen the violence up close, buried their friends, and continued to show up anyway.

From their gathering, a vision took shape: an organization that would put sex workers first. Not their numbers. Not their data. Their lives.

KISWA Is Born — 2014

In 2014, the Kisumu Sex Workers Alliance (KISWA) was formed as a coalition of sex worker-led groups across the Nyanza Region. Two years later, in July 2016, KISWA was formally registered as Kisumu Central Smart Women Against Violence and HIV/AIDS, with its office in Kisumu town.

Today, KISWA unites 22 registered sex worker-led groups across five counties — Kisumu, Siaya, Homa Bay, Migori, and Kisii. It is a non-profit, non-political feminist organization driven by one unwavering purpose: the health, legal rights, and human dignity of sex workers.

What We Fight For

KISWA's work spans five areas: awareness and sensitization, advocacy and partnerships, health care access, socio-economic empowerment, and organizational strengthening. But at the heart of it all is a simple, radical belief:

Sex workers are full human beings, deserving of rights, safety, dignity, and care.

That belief was radical enough to start a movement. And it is radical enough to keep it going.

This is our story. This is KISWA.
